note: Dates/historical identities reflect the historicist reading of the existing studies; not independent claims that dates appear verbatim in Bible passages.

notes.title: Where the seventy weeks begin
notes.text: In the historicist chronology used in these studies, Artaxerxes’ decree recorded in Ezra 7 is dated to 457 BC. The seventy weeks are understood as 490 prophetic years. Present the starting date as a historically dated decree, and the year-day method as an interpretive step—not as a date printed in Daniel.

notes.title: Messiah at the centre of the timeline
notes.text: This interpretation places the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry and anointing in AD 27, His crucifixion in AD 31, and the closing of the seventy weeks in AD 34, associated with Stephen and the wider spread of the gospel. Explain the scriptural passages alongside each historical identification.

notes.title: What do the 1,260 years represent?
notes.text: The historicist exposition compares Daniel 7:25 with Revelation’s 1,260 days and forty-two months. The prophetic time expression, the historical application and the identification of religious powers are distinct steps that deserve careful explanation. Keep the contrast between Christ’s character and coercive authority central.

notes.title: From the seventy weeks to the 2,300-year reading
notes.text: The studies connect Daniel 9 and Daniel 8 using the prophetic day-year interpretation. Beginning with the decree dated to 457 BC, the longer period is understood to reach AD 1844. Neither the year 1844 nor the completed arithmetic is printed directly in Daniel 8:14; show the steps by which the interpretation reaches that conclusion.

notes.title: What is believed to begin in 1844?
notes.text: Within the Adventist historicist reading, 1844 marks the beginning of the pre-Advent judgment phase of Christ’s heavenly ministry, not His visible return. Christ’s sacrifice at Calvary is understood as complete and sufficient; the ongoing priestly ministry applies its benefits. This distinction is important when teaching the heavenly sanctuary.

notes.title: What should the judgment message produce?
notes.text: The practical emphasis is trust in Jesus as High Priest, a willingness to be honest about sin, and assurance in God's mercy. A prophecy lesson should lead to worship and readiness to meet Christ, not simply confidence in a date. The Revelation narrative links the judgment-hour message to the everlasting gospel.

notes.title: The heavenly court and the Son of man
notes.text: Daniel 7:9–14 depicts a heavenly court and the Son of man receiving dominion; Revelation 14:6–7 joins the judgment hour to the everlasting gospel. The teaching should explain how these passages are related rather than treat judgment as separate from the character and saving ministry of Jesus.

notes.title: The issue is allegiance
notes.text: Revelation 13 portrays compelled worship and the mark; Revelation 14 presents the everlasting gospel, the Creator, and faithfulness to Jesus. Explain symbolic identifications as the prophetic interpretation used by the study, and avoid turning the teaching into judgment of the conscience of individual believers.

notes.title: The outcome is not evil's victory
notes.text: Daniel's judgment scene and Revelation's picture of Christ's victory help show why the great controversy is about God's character and His answer to evil. The teaching goal is to invite trust in Christ's self-giving love, not to focus only on the workings of Satan.
